title: Harvard Urges International Students to Return Before September 15 as New Visa Rule Takes Effect
excerpt: The university's International Office advises F-1 and J-1 visa holders to be physically present in the U.S. when DHS replaces open-ended stays with a four-year cap, warning that re-entry after the deadline triggers the new framework.
body:
• Harvard's International Office urged all F-1 students and J-1 scholars in on-campus fall programs to be physically present in the United States by September 15, when a new DHS rule replaces open-ended "duration of status" with a four-year cap on stays.
  • Students who leave the country and re-enter after the effective date will immediately fall under the new framework, which requires extensions of stay from USCIS and shortens grace periods from 60 to 30 days.
  • A coalition including the Presidents' Alliance, NAFSA, and Massachusetts colleges filed a lawsuit on August 18 seeking to block the rule, but the outcome remains uncertain and Harvard said it has no immediate effect.
  • The median time to complete a PhD in the United States is 5.7 years — well beyond the four-year cap — raising concerns that doctoral and postdoctoral students will face the heaviest administrative burden.

What Changed

The Department of Homeland Security finalized a sweeping overhaul of immigration rules for international students on July 17, ending the decades-old "duration of status" system that let F-1, J-1, and I visa holders remain in the country for the length of their programs with no fixed departure date. Under the new rule, which takes effect September 15, most new admissions will carry a maximum stay of four years or the length of the program, whichever is shorter.

https://x.com/htTweets/status/2090649681940672831

Harvard's International Office issued an August 19 advisory recommending that all F-1 and J-1 students enrolled in on-campus programs for the fall semester try to be physically present in the United States on the effective date. The reason: students and scholars already in the country on September 15 will be authorized to remain without filing an extension of stay until either their program end date or the expiration of post-completion work authorization, up to a maximum of four years from September 15.

"We recommend that J-1 scholars and F-1 and J-1 international students registered in on-campus programs for the fall term try to be physically present in the United States on the rule's effective date."

— Harvard International Office, August 19, 2026

The Travel Trap

The critical detail in Harvard's guidance is about re-entry. Any student or scholar — including those who were physically present on September 15 — who leaves the United States and returns after the effective date will fall under the new rule upon reentry. Their Form I-94 will be stamped with a specific Admit Until Date rather than the open-ended D/S notation, and their future extensions and grace periods will follow the new framework.

International travel after September 15 may also change the Admit Until Date on a student's I-94 to match the program end date on their I-20 or DS-2019, potentially affecting how future extensions are processed, according to Harvard's advisory.

What the New Framework Looks Like

Under the finalized rule, students who need additional time beyond four years must apply to USCIS for an Extension of Stay and demonstrate a compelling reason for approval. USCIS will grant an automatic 240-day extension while an application is pending. The grace period after program completion drops from 60 days to 30 for F-1 visa holders.

Graduate students are prohibited from changing their "educational objectives" — defined as educational level or major — at any point. Undergraduate students face the same restriction during their first year absent extenuating circumstances. Students who complete a degree cannot pursue another at the same or lower level.

After March 18, 2027, students transitioning into Optional Practical Training will need to apply for a separate extension of stay and work authorization — a step that was not previously required, according to the American Institute of Physics.

Why PhD Students Are Most Exposed

The National Science Foundation's 2024 Survey of Earned Doctorates found that the median time to complete a PhD across all disciplines is 5.7 years, well beyond the four-year cap. An AIP analysis found that roughly 97% of international students take more than four years to finish a doctoral program.

"For decades, foreign students have been admitted into the US indefinitely, allowing thousands to abuse our immigration system by perpetually enrolling in courses to avoid having to leave."

— Markwayne Mullin, DHS Secretary

Universities and scientific organizations have warned that the administrative burden of filing extensions — combined with processing delays and fees — could deter top talent from choosing American institutions. NAFSA called the rule a source of unnecessary uncertainty. Brookings researchers noted that USCIS now has the power to block F-1 visa holders from OPT after graduation, potentially disrupting the pipeline of STEM talent into the U.S. workforce.

Legal Challenge Filed

On August 18, the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, and NAFSA filed a lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Boston seeking to invalidate the rule. The plaintiffs also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction that, if granted, would suspend the rule during litigation.

Harvard acknowledged the lawsuit but cautioned that it has no immediate effect and that the outcome remains uncertain. The university said it would monitor the case and communicate any impact on guidance.

What Students Should Do Now

For Indian students — who represent one of the largest international student populations in the United States — the implications are direct. Those pursuing multi-year graduate programs, particularly in STEM, face the prospect of filing and paying for extension applications mid-program. Dual-degree students face additional uncertainty, as Harvard said it is still working to understand how the rule affects joint and dual-degree programs.

The advice from Harvard and peer institutions is clear: be in the country on September 15 if at all possible. Students abroad should plan their travel accordingly and consult their school's international office before booking return flights.
